title: NowSecure Benchmark Finds 97% of Mobile Applications Lack Post-Quantum Cryptography Ahead of Mandated Timelines - Quantum Computing Report
gist: NowSecure scanned 136,711 iOS and Android apps over the 90 days to October 5, 2026 and found that 96.9% show no detectable post-quantum cryptography, while more than 3,100 still run broken ciphers such as DES and RC4. It blames compiled third-party SDKs that SAST and SBOM scans miss. With EO 14412 deadlines for federal quantum-safe key establishment (2030) and signatures (2031), and a GAO audit finding none of 24 agencies fully prepared, NowSecure recommends a two-year migration cycle ahead of 2028 milestones.

insights.claim: NowSecure analyzed 136,711 unique iOS and Android apps over the 90 days ending October 5, 2026 using static binary inspection and runtime testing. 96.9% showed no detectable post-quantum cryptography code or libraries, and only 3.1% (4,241 apps) had PQC detected.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Mobile PQC migration has barely started, a large addressable market for mobile AppSec and crypto-agility vendors.
insights.locator: Evaluating 136,711 unique iOS and Android applications

insights.claim: Fewer than 1 in 10 top US mobile apps contain quantum-resilient code, and the presence of PQC code in a binary does not guarantee it executes at runtime.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Even the 3.1% headline likely overstates real protection, so runtime verification tooling has value beyond static scans.

insights.claim: Runtime testing found more than 3,100 mobile apps still using obsolete ciphers such as DES and RC4, which are open to immediate classical attacks. Many organizations must fix basic cryptographic hygiene while also planning quantum-safe crypto-agility.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Present-day exploitable crypto flaws create near-term remediation budgets, not just long-dated quantum spend.

themes.theme: Why mobile is a blind spot

insights.claim: Enterprise cryptographic inventories usually catalog server certificates and web backbones but routinely leave out mobile endpoints that handle logins, payments and encrypted communications. Because mobile traffic crosses untrusted cellular and Wi-Fi networks, apps are especially exposed to Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) collection that would be decrypted once a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: HNDL means the risk is already accruing today. This strengthens the case for early PQC spending on mobile channels at banks and payment firms.
insights.locator: The findings spotlight a critical blind spot

insights.claim: A large share of mobile encryption runs through third-party SDKs and compiled libraries (analytics, payment gateways, ad trackers) that developers do not write. SAST and SBOM dependency scans inspect source repositories and often miss the compiled cryptography in store-ready binaries, which stalls PQC rollout.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Binary-level analysis vendors gain an edge over source-code scanning tools for PQC inventory, and SDK vendors become a migration bottleneck.
insights.locator: A central driver of this lag is software architecture

insights.claim: Most commercial mobile apps secure authentication, transaction signing and TLS with RSA and ECC, which are vulnerable to Shor's algorithm. NIST standardized FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) in August 2024, yet practical mobile implementation has stalled.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Standards are settled, so the barrier is execution. Spending will go to implementation and inventory, not algorithm selection.
insights.locator: The “Mobile Gap”: Why Source Scans Miss Asymmetric Vulnerabilities

insights.claim: US Executive Order 14412 requires federal agencies to move high-value systems to quantum-safe key establishment by December 31, 2030 and to quantum-safe digital signatures by December 31, 2031. Google has set 2029 as its internal PQC migration target.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Fixed federal deadlines and Google's earlier target set the PQC demand curve for 2027-2031 and pull spending forward for federal contractors.
insights.locator: Regulatory Alignment and the Two-Year Migration Runway

insights.claim: A GAO audit released in October 2026 (GAO-27-108740) found that none of 24 major federal agencies have fully implemented essential PQC preparation practices, citing resource and inventory bottlenecks.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Federal unreadiness against hard deadlines implies a surge in government PQC procurement for inventory and migration services.
insights.locator: Federal audit data released by the Government Accountability Office

insights.claim: Gartner warns that CISOs who delay PQC planning risk compounding remediation costs as Q-Day approaches.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Analyst-firm pressure accelerates enterprise budget allocation to PQC.

insights.claim: NowSecure recommends that enterprise AppSec leads run a structured two-year migration cycle: catalog compiled binaries (first-party and vendor-supplied), audit third-party SDK roadmaps, and retest cryptographic runtime behavior on physical devices ahead of 2028 deployment milestones.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: This frames 2026-2028 as the mobile PQC remediation window, which aligns with NowSecure's own product and should be read as vendor-motivated.
